# Bioresorbable Vascular Scaffolds in Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: A Narrative Review

## Introduction and rationale

Permanent metallic drug-eluting stents (DES) revolutionised percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) but leave a durable foreign body within the vessel wall. The permanently retained metallic stent and its polymeric coating cause persistent inflammation—driving neoatherosclerosis, restenosis and late stent thrombosis—while eliminating local vasomotor function. Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) were conceived to provide transient mechanical support and drug delivery before disappearing, theoretically restoring vasomotion and remodelling. Bioresorbable scaffolds have been developed to overcome the limitations of permanent stents, to avoid the creation of permanently caged vessel segments with inhibition of vasomotion and vessel remodelling, and to avoid chronic vessel wall inflammation or long-term stent crushing and fractures [1]. Most devices consist of either a bioresorbable polymer or a bioresorbable metal alloy [2].

## The Absorb device and early evidence

The first-in-human ABSORB cohort established proof of concept. A fully bioabsorbable drug-eluting coronary stent that scaffolds the vessel wall when needed and then disappears once the acute recoil and constrictive remodelling processes have subsided has theoretical advantages; the bioabsorbable everolimus-eluting stent has a backbone of poly-L-lactic acid that provides the support and a coating of poly-D,L-lactic acid that contains and controls the release of everolimus [3]. Two-year imaging data supported feasibility [4]. The poly-L-lactic acid Absorb device provides early drug delivery and mechanical support functions similar to metallic drug-eluting stents, followed by complete bioresorption in approximately 3 years with recovery of vascular structure and function [5], and it became the only US FDA-approved scaffold [6].

## Randomised trials versus everolimus-eluting stents

ABSORB II compared the scaffold against a cobalt-chromium everolimus-eluting stent (EES). At one year, the everolimus-eluting bioresorbable scaffold showed similar 1-year composite secondary clinical outcomes to the everolimus-eluting metallic stent [7]. However, the three-year results were disappointing: the trial did not meet its co-primary endpoints of superior vasomotor reactivity and non-inferior late luminal loss, and a higher rate of device-oriented composite endpoint due to target vessel myocardial infarction was observed in the Absorb group [8]. The pivotal ABSORB III trial randomised 2008 patients and met its one-year non-inferiority endpoint [9], but 3-year adverse event rates were higher with BVS than EES, particularly TVMI and device thrombosis [10]. Five-year data extended these observations across the resorption window [11].

Real-world experience reinforced concerns. In the all-comers AIDA trial, there was no significant difference between the two study groups with respect to the primary outcome of target-vessel failure, but treatment with the bioresorbable scaffold was associated with a significantly higher incidence of overall and very late device thrombosis than the metallic stent through 2 years [12]. The final five-year AIDA report concluded that the excess risk of the Absorb BVS on late adverse events, in particular device thrombosis, in routine PCI continues up to 4 years and seems to plateau afterwards [13]. The COMPARE-ABSORB trial in high-restenosis-risk patients was discontinued prematurely because of a high thrombosis and TVMI rate in the BVS arm [14].

## Pooled and meta-analytic evidence

Pooled patient-level analyses clarified the temporal risk pattern. A one-year meta-analysis showed broadly comparable efficacy [15], but an early randomised-trial meta-analysis found that patients treated with a bioresorbable vascular scaffold had an increased risk of subacute stent thrombosis [16]. The two-year individual-patient analysis of seven trials reported that BVS use was associated with increased 2-year rates of the device-oriented composite endpoint, patient-oriented composite endpoint, target vessel-related myocardial infarction, and ischaemia-driven target lesion revascularisation [17]. A three-year pooled analysis confirmed higher 3-year rates of target lesion failure (11.7% versus 8.1%) driven by myocardial infarction [18]. A dedicated meta-analysis highlighted that the excess risk of BVS relative to EES for stent thrombosis through 2 years was significant [19], and a network meta-analysis of 91 trials found that patients treated with the Absorb BVS had a significantly higher risk of definite or probable scaffold thrombosis compared to metallic DES, with the risk of very late scaffold thrombosis highest with the Absorb BVS [20].

The final report of the ABSORB programme, pooling 5988 patients, found that between 0 and 5 years TLF occurred in 15.9% of BVS patients versus 13.1% of EES patients, but the period of excess risk ended at 3 years, the time point of complete scaffold bioresorption [21]. A broader meta-analysis was less optimistic, concluding that BVS were inferior in safety and efficacy domains at all timepoints out to 5 years, driven by an elevated rate of stent thrombosis [22].

## Mechanisms and refinement of technique

Thick struts, suboptimal implantation and incomplete resorption underlie the adverse signal. The higher scaffold thrombosis rates were likely due in part to bioresorbable polymers having insufficient radial strength, necessitating larger strut profiles [23]. Histological work showed that at 3+ years post-BVS, the majority of stented segments still demonstrated visible struts with significant neointimal proliferation by way of a predominant fibrous healing pattern [24]. The ABSORB IV trial therefore tested optimised implantation in larger vessels, including patients with myocardial infarction previously excluded [25]; midterm meta-analytic data continued to confirm increased adverse events [26], and the device-oriented composite endpoint signal persisted in further pooled analyses [27].

## Next-generation scaffolds

Interest has shifted to magnesium-based scaffolds. The sirolimus-eluting Magmaris scaffold showed favourable early outcomes in BIOSOLVE-II [28], and pooled BIOSOLVE-II/III data demonstrated good 12-month performance [29]. The large BIOSOLVE-IV registry concluded that it showed good safety and efficacy outcomes, confirming a safe rollout of the Magmaris into clinical practice [30].

## Conclusion

First-generation polymeric BVS did not deliver their promised long-term advantage, instead conferring excess myocardial infarction and scaffold thrombosis during resorption. Better strut technology, refined implantation and magnesium platforms offer a path forward, but bioresorbable technology remains investigational pending robust late-benefit data.
